title: Passover: leading a seder
hookLine: anyone can lead a seder with a simple Haggadah
tomorrow: can you add your own question to an old script?

cards: Here's an odd stage direction for a dinner party. The seder's script expects a child to ask why tonight is different. So the Talmud asks the obvious next question: what if there's no child at the table?
Its answer gets stranger as it goes. Then a spouse asks. If there's no spouse, you ask yourself.
And two scholars who already know every answer still ask each other. A person alone at a table, asking out loud why this night is different. Why would a script keep going when nobody's there to ask?

teach.b: The Torah gives the job in one line: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt."

The book that runs the night is the Haggadah, from the Hebrew for telling. It's a script with stage directions: bless the wine, wash hands, dip a green vegetable, break the matzah, ask, tell, eat, sing.
The Mishnah adds that if the child doesn't know how to ask, the parent teaches them. Now the puzzle solved.
The Talmud, in Pesachim, follows the question all the way down, from a child to a spouse to yourself to two scholars, because the seder isn't a test of whether the leader knows enough.
It's a promise that the story gets told out loud, by whoever is there. That's why anyone can lead one.
A simple Haggadah, a few people, the questions read in English, a short telling, the meal. Some seders run late into the night with commentary.
Some are short, with a toddler under the table. Both are seders. The leader's real job is small and doable: keep the questions coming, and make sure the story gets said.

how: At a Passover seder, one person usually leads from a Haggadah while everyone reads parts; seders range from long nights of commentary to short ones built around young children.

games.q: your seder: three guests, nobody under twenty, and your cousin says skip the questions, they're for kids. what does the Talmud say?
o: ask them anyway: even two scholars ask each other.
skip them: the questions are for when a child is there.
keep them, but only the youngest adult may ask.
games.why: the Talmud follows the questions all the way down: a spouse, yourself, two scholars. the questions are how the story gets told.

practice: Take a scrap of paper and write three short lines: what you'll bless, what you'll ask, what you'll eat. That's the bones of a short seder: the wine and its blessing, the questions and the story, then the meal.
Read your three lines back once, slowly, and notice that the whole night fits on one small page.

wordCard.voice: Passover: the festival of the exodus, and its seder, a night run by a script made of questions, the Haggadah.
